parts.question: Robert the Bruce was mythically inspired by one of these animals to keep fighting the English. In Akan (uh-KON) folklore, the trickster god and master of all stories takes the form of one of these animals and is named Anansi. A woman was punished for her skillfully woven depictions of the gods’ abuse by being turned into one of these animals by (*) Athena. Arachne was turned into, for ten points, what kind of eight-legged critter?

parts.label: L
parts.question: The god Iktomi usually takes the form of this animal, and inspired the creation of hoops holding string nets that are used as protective charms for children. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name these web-spinning creatures.

parts.label: B
parts.question: Iktomi appears in the religious tales of this Native American people, who make up the Sioux people with the Dakota.

parts.label: C
parts.question: Other Native American religions feature this cunning character, who is named for and behaves like a common wild canine.

topics.description: A vector physical quantity describing the rate of change of displacement, including both an object's speed and direction.

parts.label: L
parts.question: For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name these curved paths caused by gravitational interactions. They include the Earth’s trajectory around the Sun and the Moon’s trajectory around the Earth.

parts.label: B
parts.question: The efficiency of an orbital maneuver is typically measured by a value denoted “delta-[this quantity].” This quantity is squared and divided by radius to give centripetal acceleration.

parts.label: C
parts.question: Because delta-v budgets are limited, spacecraft may use these maneuvers to change speed without expending fuel. These maneuvers involve flying close to a massive object and using its orbital motion to modify the path of the spacecraft.
parts.answer: gravity assists [or gravitational slingshots; or swing-bys; prompt on fly-bys]

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: This quantity for a liquid falling out of a tank is equal to the square root of 2gh by Torricelli's theorem. Centripetal acceleration is equal to this quantity squared over radius. An object in free fall will accelerate until it reaches a “terminal” (*) type of this quantity. Because this quantity has a magnitude and a direction, it is differentiated from speed. For 10 points, name this quantity which equals the rate of change in displacement.

topics.description: A dense metallic chemical element with symbol Hg that is liquid at standard temperature and pressure.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Answer the following about electrolysis, for 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [M] In contrast to a galvanic cell, an electrolytic cell requires energy to be inputted because the change in this quantity is greater than zero, meaning the reaction is not spontaneous.
parts.answer: Gibbs free energy [prompt on delta G]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] The Caster-Kellner process uses electrolysis to isolate sodium and chlorine from salt water, using a cathode of this metal that is liquid at room temperature.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [H] This English scientist pioneered the use of electrolysis to isolate various metals. This man discovered sodium, potassium, and calcium, among other elements.

parts.label: L
parts.question: At standard temperature and pressure, only two elements are liquid. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [E] Name this metal, which is liquid at room temperature. Also known as quicksilver, this metal is symbolized Hg.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [H] Bromine, the only other element that is liquid at STP, is in this group of elements. This group features the element with the highest electronegativity.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [M] Halogens typically feature seven of these electrons, which are in the outer shell of an atom.

topics.description: A high-level programming language known for readable syntax, indentation-based code blocks, and broad library support.

parts.label: L
parts.question: A 2016 study estimated that this value was less than three for 65 percent of 133 popular GitHub projects. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] What value, defined as the minimum number of project members that have to suddenly disappear before the project is stalled, draws its name from members being hit by a certain vehicle?
parts.answer: bus factor [accept bus problem; or bus number; or lottery factor; or truck factor; or truck number; or lorry factor]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] The bus factor is a measurement of this quantity, which is how likely losses are. Investors often perform an analysis of this quantity and reward.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [M] In the first notion of the bus factor, Michael McLay theorized what would happen to this computer language if Guido van Rossum was hit by a bus. Lines in this whitespace-dependent language do not end with a semicolon.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: Users of this language can use the command “pip” to install external modules. Instead of curly brackets, this language uses syntactic indentation to distinguish blocks of code. This programming language emphasizes human readability and uses keywords like (*) “and” and “not” instead of symbols. For 10 points, name this popular programming language named after a British comedy group that shares its name with a type of snake.

topics.description: English theoretical physicist and cosmologist known for his work on black holes, cosmology, Hawking radiation, and science popularization.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: This man lost a bet to Kip Thorne regarding the binary star system Cygnus X-1, which he wrote about in A Brief History of Time. This man’s work on black holes led him to theorize a process by which they would vanish, his namesake (*) radiation. Despite suffering from a certain disorder, this man was still able to communicate using a voice synthesizer. For 10 points, name this English physicist, who passed away in 2018 due to complications of ALS.

parts.label: L
parts.question: This book contains only one equation because its author believed that every equation would cut its readership by half. For ten points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Name this book whose chapters include The Origin and Fate of the Universe and Space and Time. This book was written after its author was diagnosed with ALS.
parts.answer: A Brief History of Time: From the Big Bang to Black Holes

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] A Brief History of Time contains two chapters on these astronomical objects. These regions of space have a gravitational pull so strong that not even light can escape from their event horizons.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [M] The movie The Theory of Everything depicts the life of this author of A Brief History of Time. A type of radiation named for this physicist is given off by black holes and causes them to lose mass.

topics.description: The practice of analyzing and deciphering encoded or encrypted communications to recover their concealed messages, often for intelligence purposes.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: Gene Grabeel led a group of people in performing this task for the Venona Project. Station HYPO helped  the American Navy win the Battle of Midway by performing this task. The US Marines employed a group of  Navajos to make this task harder for other nations. (*) Room 40, best known for this task, intercepted the secret  Zimmermann Telegram. For 10 points, name this task involving the interception and decryption of hidden enemy  messages.
parts.answer: codebreaking [or cryptanalysis or cryptography or signals intelligence or SIGINT; accept  decryption or decrypting until mentioned; prompt on reading messages or intercepting messages; prompt on  counterintelligence, espionage, or equivalents for spying by asking “what specific kind of intelligence is being  done?”; do NOT accept or prompt on “encryption," “encoding," or anything that suggests hiding a message]

parts.label: L
parts.question: To be classified as this type of procedure, you must be guaranteed to get an output and stop the computation within a finite amount of time or steps. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Give this term for a set of instructions used to perform a computation. Computer programs for solving math problems are typically described by this word, but far simpler processes, long division, can be described by this word.

parts.label: B
parts.question: This British mathematician, who was prosecuted in the 1950s for being gay after years of stellar work in the war effort, is the namesake of a hypothetical machine capable of carrying out any algorithm.

parts.label: C
parts.question: Turing and the team at Bletchley Park worked on this computational task. Their greatest success was the solving of the Enigma Cipher, after which German intelligence became compromised.
parts.answer: codebreaking (accept decrypting German messages; accept deciphering German messages; accept cryptanalysis; accept word forms and descriptions thereof)

topics.description: An analytical technique that ionizes or otherwise analyzes substances by their mass-to-charge ratios to determine sample composition and structure.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: The diameter of a carbon nanotube can be determined using a form of this technique named  for an Indian scientist. Samples may be prepared for this technique using a laser shot into a  matrix to ionize a sample with minimal fragmentation, in the (*) MALDI process. The output of a  form of this technique consists of a diagnostic region and a fingerprint region. A common form of this  technique is used to analyze the mass-to-charge ratio of ions. For 10 points, name this analytical  technique that has Raman and infrared (IN-fruh-red) variants.
parts.answer: ANSWER: spectroscopy [or spectrometry; or mass spectrometry; or Raman spectroscopy; or  infrared spectroscopy; or IR spectroscopy]

parts.label: L
parts.question: At sufficiently low concentrations, the Debye-Hückel equation can be used to calculate this quantity in an electrolyte solution. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Name this quantity which corrects deviations from a liquid solution’s ideal behavior.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] According to Debye-Huckel theory, the activity coefficient is proportional to the square root of the “strength” of these species. These species are prefixed “cat-” or “an-” depending on if their charge is positive or negative.
parts.answer: ANSWER: ions [accept ionic strength or cations or anions]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [M] The formation of ions via electrospray ionization or MALDI occurs in this laboratory technique. Molecules are analyzed based on their mass to charge ratio in this technique.

topics.description: The elementary particle associated with the Higgs field and the mechanism by which certain fundamental particles acquire mass.

parts.label: L
parts.question: In 2012, this particle was found at the Large Hadron Collider. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Name this particle whose namesake mechanism explains how W and Z bosons acquired mass.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] The Higgs Boson is thought to have a value of 0 for this property. Bosons typically have integer values of this property, an intrinsic form of angular momentum.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] The Large Hadron Collider is based in Switzerland at this facility. This facility currently hosts 23 member states and is the largest particle physics lab in the world.
parts.answer: CERN [accept European Organization for Nuclear Research]

parts.label: L
parts.question: Name some things about the founder of the Illinois Math and Science Academy: Leon Lederman! For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [M] Among Lederman’s achievements is the discovery of the “bottom” form of this particle. These fundamental particles come in six flavors and make up subatomic particles, like neutrons.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] This subatomic particle with a plus 1 charge consists of 2 up quarks and 1 down quark. The atomic number of an element equals the number of this particle in the nucleus.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [H] In a 1993 book, Lederman helped popularize the term “God Particle” to describe this particle. This particle’s namesake field gives mass to certain fundamental particles.

topics.description: A chaotic regime of fluid motion involving irregular changes in velocity and pressure, eddies, and vortices, typically at high Reynolds numbers and contrasted with laminar flow.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: The smallest scales of this phenomenon are the Kolmogorov (kul-MAH-GOR-off) microscales,  which facilitate energy cascades. Time-averaged equations such as the Reynolds-averaged Navier– Stokes (NAV-yay-stoaks) equations are used to model this phenomenon in computational fluid  dynamics. This form of (*) fluid flow occurs at very high Reynolds numbers. Eddies and vortices are  produced in this form of fluid flow, which is contrasted with laminar flow. For 10 points, name this  chaotic form of fluid flow that can cause bumpy airplane rides.

parts.label: L
parts.question: A boat’s outboard motor in water produces this type of motion, which is contrasted with laminar flow. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this type of fluid movement in which particles experience unpredictable changes in velocity and pressure. Airplanes experience this phenomenon at the boundaries of air masses moving at different speeds.

parts.label: B
parts.question: The transition from laminar to turbulent flow can be predicted using this dimensionless number named for a British physicist. For a circular water pipe, turbulence occurs when this number is greater than four thousand.
parts.answer: Reynolds number (accept Re; accept Osborne Reynolds)

parts.label: C
parts.question: The dimples on this type of ball increase its Reynolds number to about fifty thousand, greatly reducing air resistance and increasing distance when it is struck with a club such as a three-iron.

topics.description: A powered fixed-wing aircraft designed for sustained flight through the atmosphere.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: When these machines exceed the critical value of attack, it causes a dangerous situation called a "stall". A common and sometimes incorrect explanation for how these machines work invokes the Bernoulli principle to explain that the air above one part of them is less (*) dense than below, generating lift. For 10 points, what machines might be powered by jet engines and take off from runways?
parts.answer: airplanes [or aircraft; accept specific types of airplanes; accept airfoils or airplane wings or airplane propellors]

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: The earliest example of this vehicle used a canard design and was permanently disabled after four uses. The town of Kill Devil Hills now commemorates one of these vehicles that was operated for the first time in 1903 at Kitty Hawk. A pair of bicycle repairmen developed, for ten points, what type of vehicle that was first operated by the Wright brothers and is now produced by firms like Boeing and Airbus?
parts.answer: airplanes (accept any additional information relating to the Wright Flyer, as all of the clues before “Wright” is read are about them)

topics.description: An inherited classification of human blood based on red-cell antigens, chiefly the ABO and Rh systems.

parts.label: L
parts.question: It was once common for high school students to determine this characteristic for themselves in the lab using a lancet and a Coombs antibody test. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this human trait whose “O-negative” type is called the universal donor, and whose “AB-positive” is the universal recipient.
parts.answer: blood type (accept blood group; prompt on partial answer)

parts.label: B
parts.question: Blood typing is mandatory to avoid a fatal reaction during this procedure, in which a patient is given new blood intravenously from a donor.

parts.label: C
parts.question: The positive or negative designation in a person’s blood type refers to this factor, usually represented with two letters, which is named for the monkey species in which it was first observed.
parts.answer: Rh factor (accept Rh(D); accept rhesus factor)

parts.label: L
parts.question: The presence of the Rh factor protein determines whether humans have a "positive" or "negative" type of this trait. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this trait determined by which of two antigens, or both or neither, are found on the surface of certain cells.

parts.label: B
parts.question: The antigens that determine blood type can be found on red blood cells, which carry oxygen from the lungs and this gas to the lungs. Humans exhale this gas, which has the formula CO2 .

parts.label: C
parts.question: People with this blood type are known as "universal donors" because, in blood transfusions, blood of this type can be given to anyone, regardless of what blood type the recipient has.
parts.answer: O- [or O negative or O minus; prompt on O; do not accept or prompt on "O+" or “O positive” or “O plus”]

topics.description: Hard anatomical structures in the mouths of animals, typically covered in enamel and used for grasping, cutting, biting, or chewing food.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Elmer Riggs showed that two genuses from this period, Brontosaurus and Apatosaurus, were the same genus. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this middle period of the Mesozoic Era, during which sauropods were hunted by therapods like Allosaurus.

parts.label: B
parts.question: Archaeopteryx, a fossil from the Jurassic, is considered a transition between dinosaurs and this class of “living dinosaurs.” Passerines are perching examples of these animals.

parts.label: C
parts.question: Despite possessing many characteristics of birds, Archaeopteryx possessed conical examples of these structures, which birds lack. These enamel-covered structures are used by some animals to chew food.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Deposits from the GCF onto these structures cause the buildup of hardened plaque called tartar. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [M] Name these anatomical structures, which have canine,molar and incisor types.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [H] This mineralized substance on the teeth is composed primarily of hydroxyapatite and can be degraded by dental caries.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] Dental cavities can be prevented by using toothpaste enriched with an anion of this most electronegative element, with symbol F.

topics.description: The unique temperature and pressure at which a substance’s solid, liquid, and gas phases coexist in thermodynamic equilibrium.

parts.label: L
parts.question: The Ehrenfest (EE-ren-fest) classification system for these events organizes them based on the degree  of their order parameters. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [10] Name these transitions between states of matter such as melting or freezing.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [10] Phase changes can be plotted on a phase diagram. At this point on the diagram a substance exists as  a solid, liquid, and gas.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [10] A cold finger is used in a process that extracts impurities during this phase transition that carbon  dioxide demonstrates below the triple point.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Answer the following about phase transitions, for 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: This phase transition occurs when a solid transitions to a liquid. Water has a value of 0 celsius for this transition.

parts.label: B
parts.question: This phase transition occurs when a solid, such as dry ice, transitions directly into a gas.

parts.label: C
parts.question: At this point, solid, liquid, and gas phases can exist at the same time. By definition, the temperature at which  this point occurs is 0.01 celsius.

topics.description: The evolutionary process by which heritable traits that improve survival or reproduction become more common in a population.

parts.label: L
parts.question: The increasing frequency of dark-colored moths in nineteenth-century England that coincided with the spread of pollution from factories can be considered a directional example of this process. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this mechanism of evolution in which individuals with favorable traits for an environment survive longer and pass those traits to their offspring.

parts.label: B
parts.question: Unlike “directional” selection, this type of natural selection favors two extreme phenotypes. This type of selection explains why finches on Santa Cruz island have either small or large beaks, with very few having medium-sized beaks.

parts.label: C
parts.question: In some African countries like Mozambique, this trait has increased in elephant populations from five to thirty-five percent in two generations. Pressure from poachers has created a directional selection for this trait, especially in female elephants.
parts.answer: tuskless (accept any description of elephants having no tusks)

parts.label: L
parts.question: A multidimensional “landscape” named for this quantity plots genotype against it, and generally assumes that successful organisms fall into local minima. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this quantity that broadly translates to “evolutionary success,” since individuals with the greatest amount of it survive to reproduce.
parts.answer: biological fitness (accept word forms like fittest)

parts.label: B
parts.question: The concept of survival of the fittest drives this mechanism of evolution, which was postulated by Charles Darwin in The Origin of Species.

parts.label: C
parts.question: The notion that natural selection slowly explores rugged fitness landscapes, in which successful adaptations are very shallow local ditches, is challenged by this more radical theory of rapid-bursts of successful trait evolution, proposed by Stephen Jay Gould.

topics.description: An industrial process that combines nitrogen and hydrogen at high pressure, typically over an iron-based catalyst, to synthesize ammonia.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: The liquid form of this compound is used along with sodium to reduce benzene in a reaction named for Arthur Birch. An iron-molybdenum (muh-LIB-din-um) cofactor is used in the production of this compound by rhizobia (rai-ZOH-bee-uh). Deadly chloramines (KLOR-uh-meenz) are produced when this compound is mixed with (*) bleach. This compound is used to produce nitric acid in the Ostwald process, and this compound can be produced under high pressures with an iron catalyst in the Haber-Bosch (HAH-bur-BOSH) process. For 10 points, name this nitrogen- and hydrogen-containing compound with formula NH3.
parts.answer: ammonia [or NH3 until it is read]

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: Lindlar’s catalyst may be used to react this molecule with an alkyne. This molecule is produced, along with carbon dioxide, in the water-gas shift reaction. By definition, this molecule is assigned a reduction potential of zero. This molecule is combined with oxygen in fuel cells that power cars. This gas reacts with nitrogen in the Haber process to form ammonia. For 10 points, name this diatomic gas of the element with atomic number one.

topics.description: The relatively calm central region of a mature tropical cyclone, typically surrounded by the eyewall and characterized by low winds and pressure.

parts.label: L
parts.question: These weather phenomena typically form over warm water. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Name these weather phenomena rated from 1 to 5 on the Saffir–Simpson scale. They are classified as a 12 of the Beaufort scale.
parts.answer: hurricanes [accept cyclones or typhoons] [prompt tropical storms]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] This region of a hurricane is characterized by calm weather. It occurs in the center of tropical cyclones such as hurricanes.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] The lowest value of this quantity for a hurricane typically occurs in its eye. It is measured with a barometer.

parts.label: L
parts.question: The "stadium effect" commonly occurs in the center of large examples of these storms. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [10] Name these cyclonic storms formed over warm oceans and measured by the Saffir-Simpson scale, which rates them from Category 1 to Category 5.
parts.answer: hurricanes [or tropical storms, or typhoons, or cyclones]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [10] Hurricanes in the Northern and Southern hemispheres rotate in different directions as a result of this inertial effect. Contrary to popular belief, this effect does not cause toilets to flush in opposite directions in different hemispheres.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [10] The aforementioned "stadium effect" causes the wall of this part of a hurricane to be slanted. This part of a hurricane typically has no cloud cover and low winds.

topics.description: The cognitive faculty and processes involved in encoding, storing, and retrieving information, including short-term and long-term memory.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: George Miller studied this facility, which he proposed has a capacity of seven plus or minus two. The prenatal form of this facility is key to maternal attachment. Walking through a doorway creates an event boundary and files away parts of this facility, which may result in the temporary (*) amnesia of why you walked into a room. Aging is correlated with loss of, for ten points, what mental facility that allows for remembering information?

parts.label: L
parts.question: The semantic type of this process occurs when individuals consciously absorb facts and general knowledge. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [E] Name this phenomenon divided into short-term and long-term types. This phenomenon is the ability of the brain to store and recall information.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] Psychologist George Miller posited that humans’short-term memories can only retain a small amount of information, specifically this number of pieces of information, plus or minus two.
parts.answer: seven [prompt on magic number or magical number]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [H] This other psychologist studied the misinformation effect by testing the way a question’s wording affected participants’ memory of a car accident.

topics.description: The branch of philosophy concerned with moral principles, including right and wrong, virtue, duty, and moral judgment.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: One non-Chinese work titled for this subject argues that each virtue is the average of two extremes in its “doctrine of the mean.” “Of Human Bondage” is a section of a work written in “geometric order” by Baruch Spinoza on this subject. (*) Nicomachus names one of two works by Aristotle on this subject. For 10 points, name this branch of philosophy, which studies right and wrong.

parts.label: L
parts.question: This thinker introduced his idea of the categorical imperative in his Groundworks on the Metaphysics of Morals. For ten points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Name this thinker whose works in epistemology and aesthetics made him a central figure in the Enlightenment. This philosopher’s doctrine of transcendental idealism can be found throughout his Critique of Pure Reason.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] Kant was a philosopher from this country. Martin Heidegger, another philosopher from this country, had deep ties with this country’s Nazi party.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [M] Kant’s deontological theory in this field is based on the idea that nothing is “good without limitation” besides a good will. This field concerns the moral principles that govern human behavior.

topics.description: A private research university in Stanford, California, associated with major psychological studies including the marshmallow test and Stanford prison experiment.

parts.label: L
parts.question: One experiment at this university that tested delayed gratification was known as its namesake “marshmallow experiment”. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Name this private university home to psychologists Albert Bandura and Philip Zimbardo, the latter of whom conducted an experiment that ended early due to abuse among the subjects.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] Zimbardo is best known for an experiment simulating one of these institutions in a basement at Stanford. Subjects of that experiment were either assigned as guards or incarcerated criminals.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [M] Bandura ran an experiment where children beat up the “Bobo” type of these objects. The Clark couple devised that children preferred to play with a white-colored type of these humanoid toys rather than a black-colored one.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Give the following about famous psychological experiments and tests, for ten points each.

parts.label: A
parts.question: In 1972, Walter Mischel studied delayed gratification by putting one of these sweet treats in a room with a child and telling them that, if they wait a small amount of time without eating it, they’ll get an extra one.
parts.answer: marshmallow (accept additional information, like marshmallow test; accept pretzel sticks; prompt on “candy”)

parts.label: B
parts.question: In a much less whimsical experiment, this professor randomly assigned volunteers as either prisoners or prison guards, then observed five days of abuse in a simulated prison before Christina Maslach convinced him to shut down the experiment.

parts.label: C
parts.question: The 1972 marshmallow test and Zimbardo’s prison experiment were both conducted by this elite private university in California, near Palo Alto south of San Francisco.

topics.description: A form of associative learning in which a previously neutral stimulus comes to elicit a response after being paired with an unconditioned stimulus.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: This man won the 1904 Nobel Prize in Physiology for using vivisection and fistulas to study the digestive system. The concept of “reflex at a distance” was expanded on by this man, with a test in which a (*) buzzer being sounded at the same time as an assistant provided food; both the assistant and the buzzer sound triggered the salivation response. For ten points, name this Russian scientist who studied classical conditioning by feeding dogs.

parts.label: L
parts.question: UPenn professor Martin Seligman electrocuted these animals to induce learned helplessness. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name these canines studied by Ivan Pavlov.

parts.label: B
parts.question: Pavlov taught dogs to drool at the sound of a bell, demonstrating the classical form of this phenomenon, which  is contrasted with its operant form.

parts.label: C
parts.question: B. F. Skinner conditioned these animals to exhibit superstitious behavior, such as head-nodding while waiting  for food. Skinner also operantly conditioned these birds to play ping pong and guide missiles.

topics.description: A philosophical argument that seeks to establish God's existence a priori from the concept or necessary nature of a maximally perfect or greatest conceivable being.
aliases: Ontological Argument for the Existence of God

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: Avicenna argued that something which has this property necessarily must also be simple and good. In metaphysics, nominalism holds that this property only applies to particulars, not to universals. The monk Gaunilo imagined an island that clearly lacks this property to refute an argument in the Proslogion. That argument was put forth by (*) Anselm of Canterbury and claims that “that which nothing greater can be conceived” must have this property. Materialists believe that only physical things have this property. For 10 points, the cosmological, teleological, and ontological arguments are used by theists to argue that God has what property?
parts.answer: existence [or being or word forms like existing; accept reality and word forms like real]

parts.label: L
parts.question: A Peter Millican paper argues that the “one fatal flaw” in this type of argument is a failure to adequately establish the nature of its subject. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Name this type of argument. One form of it relies upon a being “of which nothing greater can be conceived” that must exist in reality because any other possible being would be inferior.
parts.answer: ontological argument [prompt on, but do NOT otherwise reveal, anything describing arguments for the existence of God] (The question refers to Saint Anselm’s version of the argument.)

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] The ontological argument supports the existence of this supernatural being. Christians like Saint Anselm believe that this being exists.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [M] This philosopher’s ontological argument claims that if God is an infinitely perfect being and existence is a perfection, then God exists. In one work, this philosopher used the example of melting wax to argue for rationalism.
parts.answer: René Descartes [ruh-NAY day-CART] [or Renatus Cartesius] (The work mentioned is Meditations on First Philosophy.)

topics.description: The democratic practice of submitting or expressing a ballot or preference to select public officials or make a collective political decision.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: Geoffrey Brennan and Loren Lomasky proposed that this activity has contrasting “expressive” and “instrumental” motivations as a solution to Downs’ paradox. A Condorcet method for this activity avoids situations similar to rock, paper, scissors. Clear preferences cannot be illustrated through this activity by Arrow’s impossibility theorem. A “wasteful” form of this activity is common in (*) “first-past-the-post” systems for it, which are contrasted with a “ranked choice” method. In the U.S., this activity takes place on the first or second Tuesday in November. For 10 points, name this activity that decides officials in a democracy.
parts.answer: voting [accept word forms like casting a vote; accept electing people or word forms such as elections]

parts.label: L
parts.question: Systems to determine the results of this action include first-past-the-post, where the candidate with the most first-place rankings wins. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [E] Name this action, in which participants in an election submit ballots which are then used to make a collective decision.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] While most of the U.S. uses first-past-the-post, elections in Maine, Alaska, and recently New York City, use this type of voting system. This term refers to any preferential voting system, such as instant-runoff voting.
parts.answer: ranked-choice voting [or RVC; accept alternative vote]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [H] This economist’s “impossibility theorem” proves that no ranked voting system can ever both respect unanimous decisions and ignore irrelevant alternatives without being controlled by a single voter.

topics.description: Margaret Mead's 1928 anthropological monograph examining adolescent development, cultural practices, and sexual norms in Samoa.
aliases: Coming of Age in Samoa: A Psychological Study of Primitive Youth for Western Civilisation

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: This thinker collaborated with James Baldwin on the work A Rap on Race. Derek Freeman claimed  people on the island of Ta’u had lied to this thinker in a work titled for her (*) “fateful hoaxing.” This thinker’s  most famous work analyzes the maturation of adolescent girls in the title location. For 10 points, name this  American anthropologist, who wrote Coming of Age in Samoa.
parts.answer: Margaret Mead [or The Fateful Hoaxing of Margaret Mead]

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: This thinker may have created the stereotype of overbearing Jewish mothers after visiting Eastern European shtetls. This thinker contrasted the peaceful Arapesh and warlike Mundugumor peoples in a book that examines the “primping” of Tchambuli men. Derek Freeman refuted this thinker’s “Fateful Hoaxing” that the taupou system only applied to nobles. Films of women holding kris daggers to their chests and dancing in Bali were recorded by Gregory Bateson and this student of Franz Boas, who observed relaxed sexual norms amongst adolescent girls on the island of Ta’u. For 10 points, name this anthropologist who wrote Coming of Age in Samoa.
parts.answer: Margaret Mead [accept The Fateful Hoaxing of the Margaret Mead]

topics.description: Policies that consider race or other historically disadvantaged or protected characteristics in education, employment, contracting, or related contexts to address discrimination or promote diversity.

parts.label: L
parts.question: This policy was at the center of the case Grutter v. Bollinger. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this policy central to the similar Gratz v. Bollinger, which ruled unconstitutional a points￾based college admissions approach.
parts.answer: affirmative action [or race-based affirmative action; prompt on racial balancing or non￾race-blind admissions or racial quotas or other descriptions of taking race into account in school  admissions]

parts.label: B
parts.question: This 1978 Supreme Court case involving a medical school declared explicit racial quotas in college  admissions unconstitutional.
parts.answer: Regents of the University of California v. Bakke (BAH-kee) [or Regents v. Bakke]

parts.label: C
parts.question: This justice's opinion in Grutter declared that affirmative action would not be necessary in 25 years.  She was the first female justice on the Supreme Court.

parts.label: L
parts.question: The Supreme Court ruled that one form of this policy had to be justified by a compelling government interest in Adarand Constructors vs. Peña. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Identify this kind of policy. These policies were also litigated in the Supreme Court cases Grutter v. Bollinger and a case brought forward by Allan Bakke.
parts.answer: affirmative action [accept race-conscious admissions or race-conscious hiring or race-sensitive admissions or race-sensitive hiring]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] Bakke sued this state’s university system after he was denied admission. A ban on racial preferences in admission in this state led to less Black and Hispanic enrollment at the Los Angeles campus of its university system.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [M] The Third Circuit Court of Appeals earlier defended this president’s Philadelphia Plan that required government contractors in the city to hire minorities. Archibald Cox, a lawyer in the Bakke case, was previously fired by this president in the Saturday Night Massacre.

topics.description: An eighteenth-century Genevan philosopher and writer whose works on political theory, education, inequality, and civil society influenced modern political thought.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Thomas Hobbes stated that humans existed in a state of “war of all against all” prior to this concept. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this so-called “contract” between a government and individuals, in which the individuals agree to give up some rights in exchange for protection of other rights.

parts.label: B
parts.question: The phrase “Man is born free, yet everywhere is in chains” opens The Social Contract, a work by this Swiss Enlightenment philosopher, who also wrote Emile and Discourse on Inequality.

parts.label: C
parts.question: In Discourse on Inequality, Rousseau discussed the rise of the “private” form of this concept. John Locke’s natural rights included life, liberty, and this concept, which refers to something owned by someone.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: One work by this thinker begins by describing how mankind disrupts the beauty of nature by cross-breeding fruit trees. This thinker argued that citizens should be required to affirm only general religious tenets as part of a civil religion. This thinker defined self-preservation and the desire for others’ approval as two forms of (*) “self love” called amour de soi (“ah-MOOR de SWAH”) and amour propre (“ah-MOOR PROP”). This thinker outlined the ideal education of the title boy in Emile. This thinker wrote that in a perfect society, citizens’self-interests would combine to form the “general will.” For 10 points, name this philosopher who wrote, “Man is born free, but is everywhere in chains” in The Social Contract.

topics.description: The observed rise in average intelligence-test performance across successive generations during much of the 20th century.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: The Flynn effect describes how measures of this concept have increased over time. A test initially created to measure this concept in children is called the Stanford-Binet test. People with high values of this concept can join organizations like (*) MENSA. Around 100 is an average score for a namesake “quotient” of this concept. For 10 points, what concept is a measure of how smart a person is?

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: Studies purporting to prove the reliability of this value by Cyril Burt were revealed to contain fabricated data. The general increase of this measurement over time was dubbed the “Flynn effect” in the 1994 book The Bell Curve. Daniel Goleman created an alternative to this measurement that focuses on (*) emotional understanding. The modern form of this measurement, created by Alfred Binet (bin-AY), normalizes values to a mean of 100. Individuals who apply to Mensa must score highly on, for 10 points, what value purporting to quantify cognitive capability?
parts.answer: IQ [or IQ test; or intelligence quotient; prompt on intelligence]

topics.description: British analytic philosopher known for influential work in ethics, intention, action, and virtue ethics, as well as translating Ludwig Wittgenstein's work.

parts.label: L
parts.question: For 10 points each, answer the following about the role of women in 20th-century Christian philosophy:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [M] Before her death in the Holocaust, Edith Stein published Finite and Eternal Being, the culmination of her attempt to synthesize phenomenology with the work of this author of the Summa Theologica.
parts.answer: (Saint) Thomas Aquinas [or Doctor Angelicus or Doctor Communis; prompt on Saint Thomas]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [H] This British ethicist was also influenced by Aquinas. This author of the paper “Modern Moral Philosophy” followed Frank Ramsey in translating much of Ludwig Wittgenstein’s [VIT-gun-shtyne’s] work into English while at Cambridge.
parts.answer: G.E.M. Anscombe [or Gertrude Elizabeth Margaret Anscombe or Elizabeth Anscombe]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] In a letter to her priest, Simone Weil [vay] wrote that she became a devout Christian while traveling the world in support of this ideology. This political philosophy seeks to abolish the government.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: A philosopher who worked full-time for this organization theorized that a full merging of all  consciousness is impending at the “omega point” in The Phenomenon of Man. This organization's  advocacy of the “double effect” doctrine is explored in the moral philosophy of the author of  Intention. A head of this organization issued (*) Evangelium Vitae (ee-van-JEL-ee-um VEE-tay) to  restate its position on abortion. Elizabeth Anscombe and Pierre Teilhard de Chardin (pee-YAIR TAI-yar  doo SHAR-duh) were 20th-century philosophers who belonged to, for 10 points, what church in which  Chardin was a Jesuit priest?
parts.answer: Roman Catholic Church [or Roman Catholicism; or Jesuits or Society of Jesus until  “Fides” is read]

topics.topic: Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act
topics.description: A provision of U.S. law that generally shields online service providers from liability for user-generated content while permitting them to moderate that content.

parts.label: L
parts.question: In an analysis of this person's laptop, The Washington Post was unable to verify most of the data as  being authentic. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [10] Name this son of the current President of the United States.
parts.answer: Hunter Biden [or Robert Hunter Biden; prompt on Biden]

parts.label: B

parts.question: One provision in this section allows platforms to proactively block content that might be abusive or harmful while still being legal, without fear of liability. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Name this U.S. Code section that provides immunity for websites from liability arising from users’ posts. Criticisms of this section include that it enables hate speech or that it causes anti-conservative bias.
parts.answer: Section 230 [or Title 47 U.S. Code Section 230; prompt on the Communications Decency Act of 1996 or the Telecommunications Act of 1996]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] Donald Trump filed an executive order in May 2020 trying to change Section 230 in response to this platform’s marking of his “disputed claims” about mail-in voting. This platform has a 280-character limit on posts.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [M] This Republican senator attacked Section 230 through a bill that would require platforms to be “politically neutral.” This Missouri senator, often a critic of “Big Tech,” saluted the protestors who attacked the Capitol on January 6.

topics.description: A major Bantu language of East Africa that serves as a lingua franca across Tanzania, Kenya, and other parts of the region, including the Swahili Coast.

parts.label: L
parts.question: In his pseudo-historical book 1421, Gavin Menzies claimed that an explorer from this dynasty visited the Americas before Christopher Columbus. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [M] Name this Chinese dynasty, renowned for its blue and white porcelain, which succeeded the Yuan dynasty and preceded the Qing dynasty.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [H] The aforementioned explorer, Zheng He, brought exotic animals to China from the East African coast with this name. The Bantu language of this name is the most widely spoken in Africa.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] Zheng He made his massive voyages using junks, a type of this vessel. Lateen sails helped merchants and sailors cross the Indian Ocean in these vessels during monsoon season.

parts.question: A region named for this language contains the modern descendant of the biblical city Ophir  (oh-FEER), called Sofala (soh-FAH-lah), which was once part of the Kilwa (KEEL-wah) Sultanate.  Arab traders captured Zanj (zunj) slaves from a region named for this language. A word in this  language named a set of villages established by the Arusha (ah-ROO-shah) Declaration called  ujamaa (oo-jah-MAH), as proposed by Julius (*) Nyerere (nuhr-AIR-ay). A “Coast” named for this  language was a hub of the slave trade around the cities of Dar es Salaam (DAR-es-sah-LAHM) and  Mombasa (mahm-BAH-suh). topics.description: The number of people living in a specified geographic area, especially a country or the world, as studied in demography.

parts.label: L
parts.question: An increase in this quantity is associated with economic growth in a country. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this quantity that is a measure of the total value of goods and services produced in a country. This value is typically used by economists as a rough measure of how a country’s economy is performing.

parts.label: B
parts.question: Dividing GDP by this value for a country gives the GDP per capita, which is used to measure the standard of living of the country’s citizens. This is the measure of the number of people in a country.

parts.question: GDP can be calculated via the expenditures method by summing consumption, investment, net exports, and this value. The national debt increases when this value exceeds tax revenue. A description is acceptable.

parts.question: In his Essay on the Principles of [this quantity], Thomas Malthus claimed that this quantity’s growth  would cause poverty. topics.description: An ethical theory that evaluates actions or policies by their consequences, seeking to maximize overall happiness, well-being, or utility.

parts.question: A variant of this thought experiment involving pushing a “fat man” was created by Judith Thompson. For 10 points each:

parts.question: [E] Name this philosophical dilemma, in which pulling a lever can make the namesake vehicle kill only one person instead of five.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] Proponents of this ethical theory based on the “greatest happiness for the greatest number” would argue to pull the lever. This school of philosophy is supported by John Stuart Mill and Jeremy Bentham.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [H] Unlike utilitarianism, proponents of deontological ethics would argue to do nothing. This German thinker used the categorical imperative as the basis for deontology in The Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals.

parts.label: A
parts.question: [M] The Robinson-Patman Act forbids price discrimination if it hinders this phenomenon. Markets characterized by the “perfect” form of this phenomenon can’t engage in price discrimination because individual firms have zero market power.
